title: Lakshya Sen Lost in the Singapore Open Quarterfinals Again. India's Men's Singles Problem Is Bigger Than One Player.
excerpt: The 24-year-old fell to Japan's Koki Watanabe in three games. No Indian singles player — man or woman — reached the semifinals. With the 2028 Olympics two years away, the pipeline behind Sen remains thin.
body:
Lakshya Sen lost 21-19, 15-21, 21-15 to Japan's Koki Watanabe in the quarterfinals of the Singapore Open on Friday. The match lasted just over an hour. The result means no Indian man or woman reached the singles semifinals at this Super 750 event — a disappointing outcome for a country that once expected to dominate the badminton world.

Sen is twenty-four years old, ranked inside the top fifteen in the world, and was supposed to be the future of Indian men's singles badminton. He still might be. But the Singapore exit, combined with a string of inconsistent results in 2026, is raising questions about when that future will arrive.

A Match He Should Have Won

The opening game told the story of Sen at his best. He matched Watanabe shot for shot, stayed in every rally, and had the Japanese player scrambling to cover the court. At 19-19, Sen had the momentum. He lost two of the next three points. One lapse. That was all it took.

The second game was clinical from Sen. He took a 6-3 lead, never let Watanabe back in, and leveled the match with a composed 21-15 performance that showed exactly why India's badminton community has invested so much belief in him. His smashes were landing. His net play was sharp. His footwork was precise.

And then the third game happened.

Watanabe came out with a different intensity in the decider, racing to an early lead and never letting Sen settle. The Indian fell behind 5-10, fought back to 11-14, but could not find the finishing gear that separates quarterfinal exits from semifinal appearances. He won just four of the last eleven points.

The Deeper Problem

Sen's quarterfinal exit would not matter as much if it were isolated. But 2026 has been a year of almosts. He reached the quarterfinals of the Malaysia Open. He reached the quarterfinals of the Indonesia Open. He reached the quarterfinals in Singapore. Each time, he found a way to lose to a player he should — on rankings, on talent, on physical ability — be able to beat.

The pattern is familiar to anyone who watched Kidambi Srikanth's career arc. Srikanth was once ranked number one in the world, won four Super Series titles in a single year, and then gradually stopped converting the big moments. He is still playing, still competitive, still respected — but the windows for major titles came and went.

Sen is not there yet. He is eight years younger than Srikanth was at his peak and has time on his side. But the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics are now the defining target for Indian badminton's men's singles hopes, and the road there runs through players like Watanabe, Naraoka, and Loh Kean Yew — all roughly Sen's age, all improving at the same rate, all hungry for the same breakthrough.

India's Singles Pipeline

Behind Sen, the picture is thin. HS Prannoy, who was India's best performer at the 2024 Paris Olympics with a quarterfinal appearance, was eliminated in the round of 16 in Singapore. Kidambi Srikanth, now 33, lost in the first round. Ayush Shetty showed promise during the Thomas Cup but remains unproven at individual events. Tharun Mannepalli has been battling injuries.

For a country of 1.4 billion people, India's inability to produce a consistent men's singles contender — someone who can reach semifinals and finals at Super 750 and Super 1000 events regularly — is a structural issue, not an individual one. The Pullela Gopichand Academy produced a generation of champions. The question is whether the next generation is being developed at the same intensity.

The NRI Angle

Badminton occupies a unique space in NRI sporting identity. It is not cricket — it does not have the massive viewership or cultural weight. But it is the sport where Indian Americans often find their first competitive outlet, in school gymnasiums and community centers across the US. Sindhu's Olympic medals turned badminton into a source of national pride. Sen was supposed to carry that torch on the men's side.

He still might. Twenty-four is young in badminton years. But Singapore was another missed opportunity, and they are starting to add up.

The semifinals continue on Saturday. India's hopes rest on Satwik-Chirag in the men's doubles and Dhruv-Tanisha in the mixed doubles. The singles courts, for now, belong to someone else.
author: Diaspora Desk
